title: Illustration
subtitle: Flat Vector & Geometric Character Studies
overview: A personal series of vector illustrations built from flat colour and simple geometry. Portraits, animals and everyday scenes are reduced to their most recognisable shapes, then given depth through shade, light and confident cropping.
problem: Most of my work is systems and interfaces, where every decision has to survive a handoff. I wanted a practice that worked the opposite way: fast, expressive, and judged only on whether the image lands in the first second. The challenge was building a consistent visual language without repeating myself.
solution: A single method applied across eight pieces: find the silhouette, block it in flat shapes, add one light source, then let the composition do the rest. Bold crops and limited palettes keep each illustration readable at thumbnail size while still feeling crafted up close.

features.title: Shape-First Construction
features.description: Every subject starts as a silhouette and is rebuilt from overlapping geometric forms before any detail is added.

features.title: Flat Colour & Light
features.description: Limited palettes with one clear light source — shadow shapes carry the depth instead of gradients or texture.

features.title: Character & Animal Studies
features.description: Roughly half the series focuses on faces and animals, testing how much can be removed before the subject loses its character.

features.title: Editorial Framing
features.description: Tight crops and negative space make each piece work as an article visual, social asset or campaign graphic.

results.description: Limited palette, shape-built forms, bold crops

sections.title: Approach
sections.content: Each piece moves through the same five stages: reference, silhouette study, shape blocking, colour, and a single lighting pass. Keeping the steps fixed made the series feel like one body of work instead of eight separate experiments — and made it much easier to spot when an image was drifting off-style.

sections.title: Constraints
sections.content: Two rules did most of the heavy lifting. No more than five colours per piece, and every form had to be buildable with the pen tool and a handful of circles. Constraints forced cleaner decisions than any amount of detail would have.

sections.title: Takeaway
sections.content: Illustration makes me a better interface designer. Deciding what to remove — from a face, a scene, or a screen — is the same skill in both disciplines, and this series gave me a low-stakes place to practise it weekly.
